Production is the creation of goods and services to satisfy human wants. It is not complete until the goods or services reach the final consumer, so production also includes activities like transportation, storage and selling that add value. Production is divided into three stages: primary (extraction of raw materials, e.g. farming, mining), secondary (manufacturing raw materials into finished goods, e.g. making garri or cars), and tertiary (providing services, e.g. teaching, banking, transport).

There are four factors of production: (1) Land - natural resources provided by nature, such as soil, minerals and water; its reward is rent. (2) Labour - human effort, both mental and physical, used in production; its reward is wages or salary. (3) Capital - man-made assets used to produce other goods, such as machines, tools and money; its reward is interest. (4) Entrepreneur - the person who organises the other three factors and bears the risk of production; the reward is profit. WAEC often asks you to list each factor with its reward.

Division of labour is the splitting of a production process into different tasks, with each worker specialising in one particular task. For example, in a bakery one person mixes the dough, another bakes, and another packages the bread. Its advantages include increased output, higher skill through repetition, and saving of time. Its disadvantages include boredom from doing the same task, over-dependence (if one stage stops, others are affected), and loss of craftsmanship. Division of labour is limited by the size of the market.
